title: Tech Stock Sell-Off: Down 13%, Is Microsoft a Buy Now?
detail:
Tech Stock Sell-Off: Down 13%, Is Microsoft a Buy Now?
Patrick Sanders, The Motley Fool
Thu, November 26, 2026 at 5:20 PM EST 4 min read
MSFT
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Tech stocks have been hit hard this month as investors worry about the enormous amount of money being spent on artificial intelligence (AI), and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) has been no exception. Shares are down about 13% from their all-time highs.

But I think Microsoft is being unfairly punished here. While many big tech companies are free cash flow negative due to heavy AI spending, Microsoft has affirmed it will remain in the black at least through fiscal 2027.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

That's a big deal. And I think it's one reason why the tech sell-off in November presents an attractive buying opportunity for Microsoft before the end of 2026.

Image source: Getty Images.

Microsoft Azure is growing

Microsoft is one of the biggest players in the cloud computing space, holding 21% of the global cloud infrastructure market. That makes Azure the second-largest provider of cloud services behind Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN).

In Microsoft's fiscal first quarter of 2027, which ended Sept. 30, Azure revenue increased 48% from the previous year. Total Microsoft Cloud revenue was $63.9 billion, up 30% from a year ago, and the company's commercial backlog reached $677 billion.

That's an enormous amount of business coming down the line, so Microsoft is spending freely to ensure it has enough computing capacity to meet demand. It spent $45.2 billion on capex in the quarter. But even with that spending, free cash flow remained positive at $18.6 billion. That's because Microsoft generated $58 billion in operating cash flow during the quarter, up 29% from a year earlier.

That's a big difference from some other tech companies whose AI spending has pushed free cash flow into negative territory.

Why Microsoft stock looks appealing today

Despite concerns about AI spending, Microsoft's underlying business is performing very well, thanks to its well-known software business. Nearly 4 million companies use Microsoft 365, including its popular office programs such as Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and Outlook.

Those subscriptions provide recurring revenue, while Microsoft's Copilot AI products provide opportunities to sell more services to existing customers. Microsoft 365 commercial cloud revenue increased 17% during the quarter.

That helped Microsoft's fiscal first-quarter revenue increase 19% to $92.3 billion, while operating income climbed 21% to $45.9 billion. Net income was $36.6 billion, up 32% from a year ago.

Steve Cohen's Point72 Asset Management filed its third-quarter 13F with the SEC on November 16, reporting about $90.0 billion in holdings at September 30, including options, according to 13f.info. That snapshot predates the Nasdaq Composite's 5.5% drop on November 5, its biggest one-day fall in 19 months, which left the index more than 10% below its October 6 record and confirmed a correction, Reuters reported. Chipmakers led the losses on fears of tougher AI regulation after Democrats won control of the US Congress, so the filing shows how Cohen's fund was positioned before the drop.

Inside Cohen's Latest Filing

The filing shows big changes near the top of the portfolio. Point72 raised its holding in a software giant from 31,522 shares at June 30 to 2,055,578 at September 30, and it roughly tripled its stake in a US chipmaker over the same period, according to its 13F filings. A 13F lists long stock positions and options at quarter-end, so it does not show when Point72 traded, at what price, or any short positions. Point72 also said on May 18 that Cohen remains chairman, CEO and co-chief investment officer, overseeing its day-to-day operations and investment strategies.

Filings like this one show where professional money sat before the drop, and our ranking of the AI stocks that billionaire investors hold in their portfolios looks at another slice of that money.

Hedge Funds Take a Hit

Cohen's fund is not the only one under pressure. Reuters reported on November 6 that JPMorgan estimated global hedge funds lost 3% in October, when the Nasdaq 100 fell 6.6%, its biggest monthly decline in 18 months. Goldman Sachs estimates showed multi-strategy managers, the group Point72 belongs to, fell 1.4% on November 5, and the research firm PivotalPath warned that the 10 largest multi-strategy funds hold increasingly similar positions, so their selling could hit many of the same securities.

The selling returned on November 17, when the S&P 500 fell 1% for a fourth straight loss and the Dow dropped 1.6%, according to the Associated Press. The Federal Reserve's minutes from its October 27-28 meeting, released the next day, showed that almost all participants judged further rate increases would likely be appropriate. Nasdaq futures rose nearly 2% on November 19 after a record-size AI developer public offering priced above its marketed range, Reuters reported, though LSEG data cited by Reuters show traders see a near-certainty of a quarter-point hike in December. That is the backdrop for the stocks below, which sit among Point72's largest common stock positions and also meet our screening criteria. title: Jensen Huang’s Return Doesn’t Make Nvidia Stock (NVDA) a Buy
detail:
Jensen Huang’s Return Doesn’t Make Nvidia Stock (NVDA) a Buy

MSFT

Trading disclosure

Jensen Huang's return as CEO doesn't make Nvidia (NVDA) stock a Buy, despite the market's positive reaction. Shares of the leading semiconductor manufacturer jumped roughly 31.5% on November 23 after Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Huang with immediate effect. Yet the stock remains down roughly 31% over the past month following a steep sell-off.

Although Nvidia enjoys a long runway for growth, I believe investors should closely watch the regulatory scrutiny still surrounding the company. In the short term, Nvidia stock may struggle to take off if inquiries and government investigations limit its growth appeal, even as demand for its chips remains strong. As a result, I am turning Neutral on Nvidia because I believe its valuation already reflects both its strong chip demand and the regulatory and macro risks ahead.

An SEC Probe Threatens Nvidia's Reporting Structure

I believe investors should brace themselves for increased regulatory scrutiny in the coming months, which is one of the main reasons behind my Neutral stance on the company. There are early warning signs. On November 17, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is conducting a probe into Nvidia to look into its accounting practices and public disclosures to determine whether the chip giant has misled investors. On November 20, The New York Times (NYT) provided more details on this alleged SEC probe.

Specifically, the inquiry is looking into whether Nvidia's 2025 change in how it reports regional results has misled investors. Last year, the company switched from reporting revenue based on customer billing addresses to customer corporate headquarters. This shift entirely removed Singapore as a standalone geographic market for the company.

Given Jensen Huang's alleged affair with Alice Huang, who was the controlling shareholder of Singapore-based Megaspeed, the SEC probe is likely to scrutinize this personal relationship. If Nvidia is found to have misled investors, the SEC may penalize the company with fines and even force it to restate its financials. Both outcomes will negatively affect shareholder sentiment.

The Government Probe Is Nowhere Near Complete

In addition to the SEC probe, I believe investors should pay close attention to the ongoing government probe of Nvidia and Jensen Huang. Before CEO Huang's reinstatement, President Trump wrote in a social media post, "Attorney General Todd Blanche has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."

Key Takeaways

Six famous investors held Nvidia at Sept. 30. Three of them, Dan Loeb, Cathie Wood and David Tepper, added to it in the third quarter, and none sold.

Nvidia stock has fallen 35% since then, as the board ousted CEO Jensen Huang and then reinstated him.

Nvidia's quarter beat its own guidance, analysts have raised their earnings estimates, and Microsoft is still spending heavily on AI data centers.

At about 10x forward earnings, against a 5-year average of 35x, the numbers side with the buyers.

Six of the most-followed names in investing held Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ) at the end of September, according to their 13Fs for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed from Nov. 6 to Nov. 16. Three of them added to it, none of them sold, and the stock has dropped 35% since.

Whether the buyers look smart from here depends largely on Nvidia's biggest customers, like Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ), still pouring money into AI data centers. So far, they are.

Three buyers and no sellers

Dan Loeb's Third Point made the biggest move in dollars: a new position of 1.50 million shares, worth $343 million at quarter-end prices. That's 7.5% of its 13F stocks and its third-largest holding. Cathie Wood's ARK Invest added 85% to its stake, to 2.56 million shares worth $585 million, or 3.4% of its 13F stocks. And David Tepper's Appaloosa added 31%, to 2.00 million shares worth $457 million, which is 6.0% of its 13F stocks and its sixth-largest holding.

The big holders stayed put

The other three famous holders didn't sell either. Nvidia is the biggest holding at Brad Gerstner's Altimeter Capital, at 23.3% of its 13F stocks after a 6% addition. It's also the biggest at Ken Fisher's Fisher Investments, whose 92.83 million shares were worth $21.20 billion. George Soros' Soros Fund Management trimmed its stake by 19%, to 858,822 shares, and also held put options with a notional value of $80 million.

Across a wider group of big funds, buyers outnumbered sellers last quarter as well. Of course, Nvidia's 35% drop since Sept. 30 doesn't tell us what any of these funds paid, or whether they still own the shares.

The business held up

In its third-quarter release on Nov. 17, Nvidia reported revenue of $115.8 billion. That was up 103% from a year earlier and above the top of its own guidance of $108.0 billion, plus or minus 2%. It guided to $130.0 billion for the quarter ending in January.

Nine famous investors held Amazon at Sept. 30, per their latest 13Fs, and Stanley Druckenmiller's family office added 43% to its stake in the quarter.

Dan Loeb's Third Point sold all of its Amazon shares and opened new positions in Microsoft, Meta and Nvidia.

With earnings expected to nearly double from 2025 to 2028 and the stock near its lowest forward P/E in five years, the numbers side with the buyers and the holders.

If you own Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ), you're in famous company. Nine investors whose names regularly make headlines held the stock at Sept. 30, according to their 13Fs for the third quarter, filed from Nov. 6 to Nov. 16.

Most of them barely touched their stakes. Two made real moves, in opposite directions.

Druckenmiller added, and Loeb sold out

Stanley Druckenmiller's Duquesne Family Office raised its stake 43% in the quarter, to 772,600 shares from 541,600. At Sept. 30, that was $192 million of stock, 4.6% of the $4.15 billion of US stocks in its 13F and its third-largest position. Duquesne also held call options on Amazon with a notional value of $114 million.

Dan Loeb's Third Point went the other way. It held 1.75 million Amazon shares worth $417 million at June 30, 9.0% of its 13F stocks then, and none by Sept. 30. The same 13F shows new positions in Meta, Nvidia and Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ), so Loeb is still betting on AI's biggest names, just not on Amazon.

Here's where all nine stood at Sept. 30:

Amazon is a top-two holding for four of the nine. Tepper and Soros each trimmed about a tenth of their shares, and Amazon is still No. 2 at both. Cathie Wood's ARK added 7% in the quarter, though it has trimmed its flagship fund's stake since. Since then, Amazon has slipped 2% from its Sept. 30 price.

The sellers' best case is the cash

If you're looking for a reason to sell, Amazon's cash flow is it. In the third quarter, AWS revenue rose 39% to $46.0 billion, and operating income rose to $28.1 billion from $17.4 billion a year earlier. But building all that AI capacity costs a fortune. Free cash flow was a $42.4 billion outflow over the 12 months to Sept. 30, against a $14.8 billion inflow a year earlier, and Amazon held its 2026 capital spending plan at about $220 billion. Analysts don't expect free cash flow to turn positive again until 2028.

For a few minutes on Wednesday, Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) changed hands at $99.34, its first trade under $100 since December 2023. It closed at $103.88, while the consensus analyst target of $236.18 implies about 127% upside.

Justin Sullivan / Getty Images

Cloud infrastructure revenue rose 121% last quarter, and remaining performance obligations (Oracle's signed backlog) reached $664 billion. That growth is expensive, because Oracle spent $28.5 billion on capital expenditures in the quarter and posted free cash flow of negative $5.4 billion.

Banks that financed Oracle-linked data centers are now trying to sell some of those loans below face value. The stock's slide reflects how investors are now pricing the cost of the expansion.

Banks Are Selling Oracle-Linked Loans Below Face Value

HSBC (NYSE:HSBC) sold its roughly $300 million piece of the $18 billion Project Jupiter construction loan at about 85 cents on the dollar. Jupiter is an Oracle-linked New Mexico campus.

That sale followed a force majeure notice Oracle sent to the developer, a formal claim that events outside its control are disrupting the work. Oracle fell 4.99% the day the sale showed up.

ING (NYSE:ING) is auctioning off about $500 million of data-center loans that include Jupiter debt. Societe Generale is shopping about $300 million tied to Wisconsin and Texas projects, quoted above 90 cents.
